title: Act III, Scene II

teacherSummary.text: Juliet impatiently waits for night and Romeo. The Nurse arrives lamenting; Juliet thinks Romeo is dead, then learns Tybalt is dead and Romeo banished. She briefly condemns Romeo, then defends him. The Nurse promises to bring Romeo to her.

segments.activity: Model the close reading of the anchor quotation using the written think-aloud below.
segments.script: First, meaning. I read “Gallop apace, you fiery-footed steeds” slowly and put it in my own words: Juliet urges the fiery horses of the sun to gallop quickly to the west so night will come and bring Romeo. Next, craft. I notice the commands and the mythic image of the sun god's chariot racing across the sky. The strongest word is “Gallop”: it shows urgency, as if she could whip time itself to go faster. Then, effect. What does Juliet's speech reveal about her longing? My answer: Juliet longs for her wedding night, not knowing Romeo has just killed Tybalt; the dramatic irony makes her joyful speech painful to hear.

middleSchool.note: Excerpt-based: read the passage aloud first; use the scaffolds; accept partial answers and build with probes.

hsFreshman.note: Use the scaffolds for literal and inferential items; require one quotation for every inferential answer.

hsSophomore.note: Require a quotation and an explanation; push evaluative answers to address a counterclaim.

hsJunior.note: Emphasize structure and ambiguity; students should name where the text leaves matters open.

hsSenior.note: Weigh competing interpretations; students should defend the stronger reading.

ap.note: Treat each evaluative item as a thesis rehearsal: defensible claim, purposeful evidence, commentary on choices.

collegeFreshman.note: Add the extension: connect answers to historical context and one secondary perspective.

collegeSophomore.note: Use the extensions: genre and period conventions, and a published critic.

collegeJunior.note: Use the extensions: name a critical method and test it against the passage.

collegeSenior.note: Use the extensions: connect the scene to the whole work and the scholarship.

graduate.note: Use the extensions: position answers in a critical conversation and the textual history.

contentNotes.teacherNote: Hearing of Tybalt's death and Romeo's banishment, Juliet says she will go to her wedding bed and let death take her maidenhead. Use the safe-messaging script; keep focus on her grief and on who could help her. The Nurse calls for 'aqua vitae' (brandy), used as a restorative after shock. Juliet's 'death, not Romeo, take my maidenhead' refers to her virginity and wedding night; she is thirteen. Gloss plainly.
contentNotes.studentPreview: A character in despair speaks about dying. Support is available if this is hard to read.
contentNotes.suggestedLanguage: “What news has crushed Juliet, and who comes to help?”

safeMessaging.teacherScript: Discuss the character's despair and what the text does with it; do not dwell on methods. Before the lesson, remind students that support is available and how to reach the counselor. Check in privately with any student who seems affected and follow your school's referral protocol.
